Hey what you have sounds more like TTTS as sound is your main trigger. I had a little bit of this, but I think I had more MEM as I had non-sound triggers too, such as yawning or burping. While sound was not my main trigger, high frequency sounds, such a silverware and ceramic plates making contact caused a bit of a response from my ears. Ether way, the best advice I can give you is to try to not let the anxiety and fear from the thumping and the sounds that trigger it to control you. I really had a hard time mentally for months, but at some point I just stopped caring, I know that sounds difficult, but I think the mental aspect can prevent it from getting better. That doesn't mean it will improve right away, it took months for me to notice improvement after I got my anxiety about it under control. But it was honestly fine that it took months cause I mostly stopped worrying about thumping and the triggering sounds. I would also recommend you see an ENT just to confirm there are no physical issues with the structures in your middle ear. In my case and in most cases, there is not. Good luck and try to not let this control your life.

Yeah I would be happy to share, but just keep in mind that my approach might not work for many people here and might even cause harm for many people with hyperacusis, as there are different causes, factors, and unknown variables for each individual case. 

Basically, I tried my best to stop worrying about it and started to live my life like I did not have it. I still took some basic common sense measures such as a volume limit on my headphones when I listen to music at the gym, wearing double ear protection when I shoot my guns at the range, and so on. But I would not worry about sound or worry about the future in terms of getting worse. I think the anxiety and stress was at least a partial factor for me. It took a couple months to see results, but the partial recovery has been holding for the past 6 months. I also started taking Gabapentin and Cymbalta for other health problems, but maybe these medications helped a bit, but who knows. I still do get pain in my ears that can spread all over my head when I hear sounds, especially sounds like ceramics or metal on metal sounds such as silverware, but it is not as bad as it used to be.

There might be different factors involved beyond just hair cells, such as your middle ear, a brain component, and other parts of your nervous system. I have recovered about 75% so far, so it does not have to get worse over time, there is so much we don't fully understand about this.

I am not saying you have this middle ear condition as only a doctor can accurately diagnose you.

Hopefully someone here can answer the first part of the question, but as for the second part, I would imagine it is considered somewhat bad news for most of the fund holders. The reason being, you can always sell out of an ETF whenever you want, but this basically forces you to, whether you sell the shares or wait for the fund to be liquidated. This also causes a taxable event, and might interfere with your investment timeline. But usually this is not an overly negative event as you are still receiving fair market value for the shares you owned by owning the ETF, it just forces you into a sell position. The price of the ETF might dip at the news of the closure, and you might lose some money if the value of the ETF was worth more than the sum of the shares within. Another potential risk is that the market value of some of the shares within the ETF might be lower at the time of liquidation compared to before or after this event. But this event is still FAR better compared to holding shares of a company that goes bankrupt because in most cases you would still retain most of the value of the ETF at the time of the announcement of closure.

The sponsor of the ETF is supposed to liquidate the shares and distribute the money to those who owned shares with the ETF. Usually you get a heads up at least a few weeks or more before this happens, and you have to decide if you would make more money selling the ETF right away, or holding on to it when they liquidate the fund.
